A-level Maths · Pure — Logarithms Simplifying a log expression into a single logarithm.  Three logs, two of them wearing coefficients, and a base nobody tells you. The order is the whole trick: clear the coefficients FIRST, because the adding and subtracting laws only work on bare logs. A half power is a square root, so ½log 256 becomes log 16 — not log 128. A 2 out front means squared, not doubled, so 2log 48 is log 2304, not log 96. Then plus becomes times, minus becomes divide, and you’re down to log of 576 over 2304 — which is exactly a quarter.  Most people stop there. It’s correct, and it isn’t finished: a quarter is four to the minus one, and the power law runs BOTH ways, so the −1 comes back down to the front. −log 4. Or −2log 2, if the paper asks for it in terms of log 2.  And you never needed to know what the base was. Not once.  #alevelmaths #logarithms #maths #mathstok

Arithmetic Series | Where the Formula Comes From  A-Level Maths, Pure — the proof of Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n−1)d], built from the sum written out in full to the formula in the box.  What you’ll learn: • why the last term is a + (n−1)d, not a + nd — the off-by-one that quietly costs marks • the one move the whole proof turns on: write the entire sum out again, upside down • why every pair across the two lists adds to the same total — whatever you gain at one end, you lose at the other • where the divide-by-2 comes from: you added two whole copies of the sum, and you watch both of them • why there’s no condition beside this formula — nothing gets divided by anything that could be zero (unlike the geometric series’ r ≠ 1)  A step that changes nothing is the hardest kind to think of trying. That’s the whole trick.  Not in this one: the Sₙ = n/2(a + l) version — same formula, one substitution away, and its own video.  #alevelmaths #arithmeticseries #alevelrevision #mathsproof #puremaths sequencesandseries

Edexcel A-level Maths · Pure Year 2 — Parametric Equations  Most people meet a parametric pair and read it as two separate things. It isn’t. It’s one point, on one set of axes, and t is the clock that drives it — which is why almost everything worth describing in maths is written this way: a golf ball, a planet, a particle in mechanics.  We start with the applications, then do the bit that trips everyone up: two objects whose paths cross are NOT colliding. One reaches the crossing at t = 1, the other a whole second later. Same place, different time.  Then the technique. Because it’s the same t in both equations, eliminating it is just algebra: x = 2t gives t = x over 2, drop that in, square the top and the bottom, and you get y = x²/4 — proved by drawing it straight over the path the point already traced. The circle needs a different route, because you can’t make t the subject of cos t: square both and use cos²t + sin²t = 1.  And the honest bit almost nobody says out loud — the Cartesian equation loses something. It can’t tell you the point goes round again, and it can’t tell you t stopped at π.  #alevelmaths #edexcel #parametricequations #mathstok

Where nCk actually comes from, derived by counting routes across a grid.  Inspired by the brilliant jayminshah.maths   You can only go right or up, so every route uses the same four rights and three ups — only the order changes. That turns a geometry problem into an ordering problem, and the grid can go. Pretend all seven moves are different and the count is easy: seven factorial, five thousand and forty. Then freeze one route and shuffle the labels on its rights. Nothing moves. That route has been counted twenty-four times, and here’s the bit that makes the whole thing work: it’s twenty-four for every route, the same overcount everywhere, which is the only reason a single division can fix it. Divide by four factorial, then again by three factorial for the ups, and thirty-five falls out. Swap the numbers for letters and you have the formula.  Two traps in here. Stopping at two hundred and ten, because you divided out one group and forgot the other — that’s the most common way this goes wrong. And subtracting the overcount instead of dividing it: labelling multiplied the count, so undoing it divides.  #combinatorics #binomial #mathstok

Heatwave incoming. Your car is about to become an oven. Here’s the thirty-second fix — and the first time anyone’s shown you why it works.  You’ve heard it by now: drop the far rear window, then waft the driver’s door. Everyone has explained it. Nobody has shown you what the air actually does.  So I simulated it. Real fluid dynamics, one horizontal slice through the cabin, seen from above. Orange is the baking air that was already in there. Blue is fresh air from outside.  Swing the door out and it works like a paddle — it sweeps the air beside the car out of the way, and the pressure across the open doorway drops. Air always gets pushed from higher pressure toward lower, so the hot air doesn’t seep out, it gets pushed out. And because the only way back in is that one window on the far corner, every bit of fresh air has to cross the whole cabin to reach you.  The number on screen is measured live from the simulation, not made up. Keep wafting and it keeps emptying — about three quarters of the air ends up new.  Trick popularised by the brilliant fryrsquared 🙏  One honest note: the air in my simulation is thicker than real air — a much lower Reynolds number than a real car door. That’s a deliberate teaching choice. Real air at this speed goes turbulent and the picture turns into a mess of eddies; slowing it down keeps the flow smooth enough that you can actually follow where each parcel of air goes. The mechanism is the same, it’s just legible.  #physics #fluiddynamics #heatwave #cfd #simulation

A-level Maths · Pure Year 2 — Integration Subtopic: integration by substitution, twice over  ∫ tan³(ln x)/x dx looks horrible until you spot the log of x sitting next to its own derivative — that pairing is the whole way in. Let u = ln x and the integral collapses to tan³u. Peel one tan off, swap the tan² for sec²u − 1, and it splits into two integrals you can actually do: one by a = tan u, the other by b = cos u. The answer lands as ½tan²(ln x) + ln|cos(ln x)| + C.  The trap is the last combine: you’re subtracting an integral whose answer is already negative. Drop one of those minuses and your final sign is wrong — plenty of textbooks have done exactly that. Differentiate your answer back if you’re not sure.  #alevelmaths #integration #calculus #mathstok

How does Bernoulli’s principle actually work?  Where a pipe narrows, the same air has to pass through less space every second. So it has to move faster. That part is just conservation of mass.  But air doesn’t decide to speed up. Like anything else, it only accelerates when something pushes it — and here that something is a pressure difference. The pressure in the wide section is higher than in the neck, so a parcel of air sitting between them is pressed harder from behind than from in front. That imbalance is a net forward force.  So the parcel accelerates, and the pressure behind it does work on it: stored pressure energy becomes energy of motion. Pressure falls exactly as speed rises. The total barely moves.  Which is why the famous line — “fast air is low pressure air” — has the causality backwards. The air isn’t at low pressure *because* it’s fast. It’s fast because a pressure difference pushed it, and the low pressure is what it paid.  That trade does real work: it draws perfume up an atomiser, pulls fuel into a carburettor, and tells an airliner how fast it’s flying.  Everything here is a real fluid simulation — a lattice-Boltzmann solve. The colours are the actual computed pressure, the arrows are the actual measured pressure imbalance, and the energy bars are the actual measured pressure and kinetic energy on one shared scale.  #physics #bernoulli #venturi #fluiddynamics #aerodynamics cfd simulation science stem engineering

Edexcel-style A-level Maths · Pure — Exponentials and Logarithms Simultaneous logarithmic equations: get everything speaking the same language, then strip the logs.  An eight-marker with two different bases, worked the way you’d actually think through it. The 1 looks separate from everything else — it isn’t, because 1 is just log base two of 2, and the same trick turns the 2 into 2 log base three of 3. Coefficients block the addition law, so both of those 2s climb up as powers before the right-hand sides collapse to one log each. Exponentiate each line by its own base and you’re left with an ordinary nonlinear pair: y = 2x + 1 into y² = 9x gives 4x² − 5x + 1 = 0, which factorises to (4x − 1)(x − 1). Both pairs survive the final check that every log argument stays positive — yes, even the fraction. Stripping too early and binning the ¼ by reflex are where the marks go.  #alevelmaths #edexcelmaths #logarithms #mathstok

How does the Magnus effect work?  Zoom in far enough and the air touching the ball’s surface isn’t moving at all — it sticks to it. That thin sticky sheet is called the boundary layer.  So when the ball spins, it drags the air around with it — as much as it can.  On one side, the surface is moving the same way as the oncoming air, so the air there gets helped along and speeds up. Faster air means lower pressure.  On the other side, the surface is moving against the air, dragging on it and slowing it down. Slower air piles up — higher pressure.  And since things get pushed from high pressure to low pressure, the ball curves.  Blue is low pressure, red is high. Watch it swerve toward the blue.  #physics #magnuseffect #football #freekick #aerodynamics cfd simulation science stem

Edexcel A-level Maths · Pure Year 2 — Exponentials and Logarithms  Exponential equations that hide a polynomial in e to the x.  This one looks nasty until you audit the powers: e to the two x is just e to the x squared, and e to the minus x is one over it. Multiply everything through by e to the x — safe, because e to the x is never zero — and substitute u for e to the x. What’s left is an ordinary cubic. The factor theorem finds y equals minus one, the rest factorises, and three candidates drop out. Only two survive, because e to the x is always positive, and the natural log brings back the exact answers: x equals minus log two, and x equals log three. The film also kills the classic slip — multiplying the left side and leaving the four alone.  #alevelmaths #edexcelmaths #exponentials #logarithms #mathstok

Geometric Series | Where the Formula Comes From  A-Level Maths, Pure — the proof of Sₙ = a(1−rⁿ)/(1−r), built from the sum written out in full to the formula in the box.  What you’ll learn: • why the n-th term is a·rⁿ⁻¹, not a·rⁿ — the off-by-one that quietly costs marks • the one move the whole proof turns on: copy the sum out again and multiply the copy by r • why that makes the two lines share n−1 identical terms, and what that overlap is FOR • exactly which terms cancel when you subtract, watched pair by pair instead of asserted • where the r ≠ 1 condition beside the formula comes from — it is earned at the divide step, not memorised  The trick took mathematicians a very long time to find. You are not supposed to spot it cold — you are supposed to understand why it works.  Not in this one: the r = 1 case (the formula doesn’t apply; the sum is just na) and the sum to infinity, which needs |r| < 1 and is its own result.  #alevelmaths #geometricseries #alevelrevision #mathsproof #puremaths sequencesandseries

A-level Maths · Pure — Proof Proof by contradiction: the cube root of 2 is irrational.  Assume the opposite — the cube root of two is a fraction a over b, fully cancelled, hcf one. Cube both sides and the claim turns into whole numbers: a cubed equals two b cubed. That right side is two times a whole number, so a cubed is even — and the only way a cube comes out even is if a itself is even. Cube an odd number, two k plus one, and a plus one survives every factor of two. Feed a equals two k back through and b is forced even as well. Both even means a shared factor of two — but we said lowest terms. The assumption breaks, and that’s the whole proof. The line students throw away? The lowest-terms clause — if your proof never uses it, the ending proves nothing.  #alevelmaths #proof #puremaths #mathstok

Edexcel A-level Maths · Pure Year 2 — Integration Subtopic: integrating with trigonometric identities  No standard result touches ∫(1+sin x)/(1−sin x) dx — so we change how it looks without changing what it is. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (1+sin x): that whole factor is just ×1, and the bottom becomes a difference of two squares. The Pythagorean identity collapses it to cos²x, the fraction splits into the sec/tan family, and 1+tan²x = sec²x finishes the rewrite: 2sec²x + 2sec x tan x − 1. Every piece is now a formula-booklet result, and the answer drops out: 2tan x + 2sec x − x + C.  Two classic traps to watch: multiplying only the denominator (that changes the function), and “integrating” tan²x with the power rule (tan x isn’t a plain power of x).  #alevelmaths #edexcel #integration #calculus #mathstok

In A-Level Further Maths, the concept of Volumes of Revolution 📐 is a powerful application of calculus. This technique involves rotating a curve around a given axis to create a three-dimensional solid, and then calculating the volume of that solid using integration.  How It Works:  When a curve is rotated about an axis, it forms a solid shape whose volume can be found by integrating the area of cross-sections perpendicular to the axis of rotation. This method is essential for finding the volumes of shapes that are not easily measurable by traditional means, especially when dealing with irregular or complex curves.  Applications in the Real World:  ⚙️ Engineering: Volumes of Revolution are crucial in the design of mechanical components such as pistons, wheels, and pipes, where the shapes are often generated by rotating a profile around an axis.  🏥 Medicine: In medical imaging and treatment, calculating the volume of organs, tumors, or implants often involves modeling these structures as solids of revolution.  🌊 Physics and Fluid Dynamics: This concept is used to determine the volume of fluids in containers, tanks, or pipes, which are typically cylindrical or spherical in shape.  🏛️ Architecture and Design: Architects and designers apply this concept when creating objects like domes, arches, and other structures that are symmetrical around an axis.  By mastering Volumes of Revolution, students develop a deeper understanding of integration and its practical applications, which are essential in various scientific and engineering disciplines. It applies standard differentiation rules to both sides of such equations, treating variables like y as functions of x, to find derivatives like dy/dx.
